The Indomalayan pencil-tailed tree mouse Chiropodomys gliroides is a small, arboreal murid rodent inhabiting the bamboo and forest understory of Southeast Asia. Neonates of this species are altricial and exhibit a modest birth mass of 2.8 grams [Wwb = 2.8 grams], a value consistent with the pattern observed in many small-bodied rodents that produce multiple offspring per reproductive effort. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a core body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], the gestation period for this species lasts 20 days [tg = 20 days] and the time since birth at weaning occurs at 24 days [tx = 24 days], a relatively short interval that aligns with the rapid reproductive cycle typical of tiny, bamboo-dwelling rodents and reflects a swift transition from maternal milk dependence to the onset of independent foraging on seeds, fruits, and tender bamboo shoots.

Females of Chiropodomys gliroides initiate their reproductive activity at a relatively early age. The time since birth at puberty for females has been recorded at 101 days [tp = 101 days] when measured at 37 °C [T = 37 °C], indicating a fairly rapid attainment of sexual maturity for a murid of its size. Following puberty, maternal investment proceeds without lengthy delay; the average litter size in this species is 2.2 pups per litter [N_R_i = 2.2 pups per litter]. Given the relatively brief gestation and accelerated juvenile development, this moderate litter output contributes to a substantial maximum reproductive rate. Adult females are capable of raising approximately 2 litters annually [F_R_i = approximately 2 litters annually], a frequency shaped by the seasonal abundance of bamboo seeds and invertebrates that fuel the energetic demands of lactation.

Adult body size in Chiropodomys gliroides is modest, with the species attaining an ultimate wet weight of 29 grams [Wwi = 29 grams], making it one of the smaller members of its genus. This diminutive adult mass is accompanied by a wet weight at weaning of 10 grams [Wwx = 10 grams], a threshold that marks nutritional independence. The transition from a neonatal mass of 2.8 grams at birth to this weaning mass involves a rapid, nearly fourfold increase in body size over approximately 24 days, a growth rate that demands intensive maternal provisioning. Comparative data from related murid rodents indicate that an asymptotic mass of 29 grams is at the lower end of the size spectrum for ground-dwelling relatives, reflecting the energetic constraints associated with an arboreal, bamboo-specialist lifestyle.

Longevity in the Indomalayan pencil-tailed tree mouse is notably extended given its small body size. Under thermoneutral conditions (37 °C [T = 37 °C]), the maximum lifespan has been documented at approximately 3.6 years [am = approximately 3.6 years], a figure that is considerably longer than what simple allometric scaling would predict for a 29-gram rodent. This extended lifespan, coupled with a moderate reproductive output of 2.2 pups per litter and a maturation age of roughly 101 days, underscores a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival over high fecundity. The species' relatively low annual mortality rate in its natural bamboo forest habitat likely compensates for its modest litter size, allowing populations to persist through periods of resource scarcity.

Field observations of Chiropodomys gliroides provide further context for its reproductive physiology. At a sustaining body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], the combination of a litter size of 2.2 pups and an interbirth interval that permits just over two litters per year yields an annual output of roughly 4.4 pups. This moderate fecundity is balanced by the species' extended potential lifespan of approximately 3.6 years under favorable conditions, allowing a single female to contribute multiple cohorts over her lifetime. The ecological correlates of this life-history pattern are evident in the species' reliance on seasonally pulsing food resources such as bamboo mast seeding events, which likely constrained the evolution of both the 20-day gestation period and the 101-day delay to female sexual maturity.
